The old lighthouse had gone dark for years, so no one expected the beam to return at midnight.  
When it did, ships saw not their own reflections but the ghosts of sailors lost at sea.  
By dawn, the lighthouse keeper was gone, leaving only a logbook that read, “I finally let them go.”

When seven-year-old Lila pried the warped, water-stained shoebox out from under the floorboards of her family’s new farmhouse, she didn’t expect to find a stack of hand-drawn star maps tucked inside, each labeled with the same looping scrawl: “Marnie’s sky.”
Her grandma, who’d been sorting old linens in the next room, paused when she saw the maps, and told her Marnie was the girl who’d lived in the house 60 years prior, the one who’d spent every summer night on that same porch tracing constellations and promising she’d leave a map for any kid who ever needed to find their way home.
That night, Lila taped the faintest, smudgiest of the maps to her bedroom ceiling, and when she looked up at the real stars peeking through her window, she could have sworn she saw the faint outline of a girl waving back from the tail of Orion.
